source: Jenner et al. (2024) Evidence of learned look-ahead in a chess-playing neural network
finding: Inside Leela Chess Zero's policy net (no external search), activations on the squares of future optimal moves matter causally. Look-ahead-like content is computed inside one forward pass.
numbers: Patching the 3rd-move target square in layer 10 cut the log odds of the correct move by 1.88 (+/-0.04, 2 SE), e.g. probability 50% to 13%. 22.5k filtered Lichess puzzles.
limits: Leela only. Puzzles kept only if Leela solves them and a weaker Leela fails; sacrifice-heavy (1st and 2nd target square the same in 83% of kept puzzles vs 47% in the raw set).
agent_relevance: Pattern recognition and search are not cleanly separate: a recognition-style net can hold future-move candidates. A fast first pass (S0) may already contain some look-ahead.

source: Jenner et al. (2024) Evidence of learned look-ahead in a chess-playing neural network
finding: One attention head (L12H12) moves information from the 3rd-move square back to the 1st-move square; ablating it hurts.
numbers: Attention entry 1st-to-3rd target is large in 29.8% of puzzles; ablating it cut log odds of the right move by more than 1.5 in more than 10% of puzzles. Ablating a piece-movement head tied to the future move cut log odds by 1.5+ in 60% of puzzles (puzzles with lines longer than 3 moves).
limits: Selected puzzles; one model family; ablation does not show the full algorithm.
agent_relevance: Supports the Gobet 1997 picture that recognition feeds a short search; both can sit in one fast pass.

source: Jenner et al. (2024) Evidence of learned look-ahead in a chess-playing neural network
finding: A simple probe on the activations predicts the optimal move two turns ahead.
numbers: 92% accuracy at predicting the move 2 turns ahead, only on states where Leela finds a single best line (70% of puzzles train the probe, 30% test).
limits: Easy single-line states; a probe shows the information exists, not that the net uses it.
agent_relevance: Test whether an LLM's first-pass answer already carries the plan before slow deliberation.

source: Jenner et al. (2024) Evidence of learned look-ahead in a chess-playing neural network
finding: Policy-only Leela is strong without search; adding value and search is stronger.
numbers: A Lichess bot using only Leela's policy net reached blitz and rapid ratings over 2600 (appendix, cited from an external page). The paper's version is roughly even with Ruoss et al.'s network on puzzles.
limits: Rating figure comes from an archived Lichess page cited in the appendix; not re-checked.
agent_relevance: Rough size of what recognition alone buys at master level.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: Table 1 splits recognition from search: the same engine with and without test-time search.
numbers: Puzzle accuracy: AlphaZero policy only 56.1%, value only 82.0%, with 400 MCTS sims 95.6%. Leela policy only 88.6% (tournament Elo 2292), value only 95.9% (2418), 400 sims 99.6% (2858). Stockfish 16 (50 ms) 99.8% (2711).
limits: Tournament Elos are internal and not comparable to Lichess Elo. Training regimes differ per engine.
agent_relevance: Search adds a lot to a weak prior (AlphaZero policy +39.5 puzzle points) and little to a strong one (Leela policy +11 points). A better cue store means less search is needed.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: A transformer trained by supervised learning to copy Stockfish action-values plays at master level with no search at test time.
numbers: 270M model: tournament Elo 2299, Lichess blitz 2895 vs humans (2299 vs bots), puzzle accuracy 95.4%. 136M: 2259 and 94.5%. 9M: 2025 and 88.9%. Trained on 10 million human games annotated by Stockfish.
limits: Lichess Elo vs humans is above the Elo vs bots; engines see only FEN and need a workaround for repetition draws.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that a large store of patterns can replace most search. Scale of stored patterns carries the skill.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized planning with large-scale transformers: a case study on chess
finding: A general language model (GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct) is far below the specialised searchless net on puzzles.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo-instruct: Lichess Elo vs bots 1755, puzzle accuracy 66.5% (PGN input, following Carlini). Ruoss 270M: 95.4%.
limits: 2023 model; PGN input; GPT-4 not tested because earlier work found illegal moves.
agent_relevance: A generic LLM has a weak chess pattern store; the store, not the search, is the bottleneck.

source: Monroe and Chalmers (2024) Mastering Chess with a Transformer Model
finding: A better position encoding (relative scheme from Shaw et al.) lets a searchless transformer match Ruoss et al. at far lower compute.
numbers: CF-240M policy: Elo 2347, puzzles 93.5%, 12.8B FLOPs; GC-270M: 2299, 93.5%, 427B FLOPs. CF-6M policy: 2105, 65.3%. AlphaZero policy: 1620, 61.0%. Shaw encoding beat learned absolute embeddings by 1.83% policy accuracy.
limits: Elo for GC and AlphaZero taken from earlier papers; internal tournament.
agent_relevance: How relations between pieces are encoded matters as much as how many patterns are stored. Supports typed slots and relations in a template store.

source: Schultz et al. (2024) Mastering board games by external and internal planning with language models
finding: A language model used as a value function plus a small search gives a big jump. Recognition guides the search; a little search finishes the job.
numbers: MAV alone: external Elo 2923 (mean scoring), 2875 (max scoring). With only 100 MCTS simulations: internal Elo 68 above searchless MAV; overall about +300 Elo with a limited search. Elo grows roughly logarithmically in simulations. 14,689 chess games in the tournament.
limits: Model pretrained on chess; authors say how to add such value functions to general chat is open.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM version of the theory: a fast learned prior prunes the tree. Argues for a cheap search step on top of recognition.

source: Schultz et al. (2024) Mastering board games by external and internal planning with language models
finding: The model can be trained to write its own small search tree in context (internal search), then pick a move. Strength rises with tokens spent.
numbers: Built the requested tree shape 99.6% of the time (5,980 positions). Elo rises with the search budget in tokens. Grandmaster-level chess at a search budget closer to a human's (abstract claim).
limits: Trained on search traces from the paper's own pipeline; the human-budget comparison is the authors' claim.
agent_relevance: A shortlist-then-shaped-tree loop inside the context window works. Cue first, then breadth and depth.

source: McIlroy-Young et al. (2020) Aligning superhuman AI with human behavior: chess as a model system (Maia)
finding: Predicting the move a human plays is better done by a recognition-style net than by a search engine. Human choice looks cue-driven.
numbers: Stockfish at depths 1-15 matches human moves only 33-41% of the time; Leela at most 46%. Maia's lowest accuracy (trained on 1900-rated, tested on 1100-rated) is 46%; highest over 52%.
limits: Single-move prediction on Lichess data in nine rating bins (1100-1900).
agent_relevance: More search does not make a model more human or expert-like. A cue-built shortlist matches expert play better.

source: McIlroy-Young et al. (2020) Aligning superhuman AI with human behavior: chess as a model system (Maia)
finding: Search depth and human skill are not aligned: stronger Stockfish does not match stronger humans more.
numbers: Accuracy is non-monotone in depth (depth 1 beats depth 5 but not depth 15). Depth 15 matches 1900-rated players only 5 points more than 1100-rated players. Stockfish strength rises largely orthogonally to human strength.
limits: Exact effect of Maia plus 10 tree-search rollouts not read in full.
agent_relevance: Skill growth in humans is more about better cues than deeper search, consistent with Gobet 1997.

source: Schut et al. (2023) Bridging the human-AI knowledge gap: concept discovery and transfer in AlphaZero
finding: Concepts found in AlphaZero's activation space, shown as puzzle positions, were learnable by top humans.
numbers: Four top grandmasters improved at finding concept-based moves after seeing AlphaZero's examples (human study, N=4).
limits: Abstract and intro read; improvement sizes not extracted. Very small N.
agent_relevance: A store of concept prototype examples can transfer expertise; the unit is a set of prototype positions.

source: McGrath et al. (2022) Acquisition of chess knowledge in AlphaZero
finding: Human chess concepts become decodable inside AlphaZero as it trains, layer by layer, with no human data.
numbers: Concept probes tracked over training checkpoints and across 20 residual blocks (what-when-where plots); includes opening-play analysis with GM Kramnik.
limits: Abstract and methods read; linear probing is correlational.
agent_relevance: Learned recognition features mirror human concepts, so a human-concept cue vocabulary is a sensible target for an agent memory.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Explore the reasoning capability of LLMs in the chess testbed (MATE)
finding: Adding a written strategy or tactic note to each candidate move helps models pick the best move. The notes act as cues.
numbers: 1 million positions with expert notes; choose the best of the candidate moves; 1000 test samples per set. o1-mini zero-shot: +14 with strategy notes, +24 with tactic notes, +34 with both over no notes. gpt-4o with both notes: +10 over tactic, +14 over strategy, +30 over none. Fine-tuned LLaMA-3-8B beat the best commercial model by 24.2% with both notes.
quote: performance improves for most LLMs we test when provided with linguistic explanations
limits: Notes come with the candidates; the model does not retrieve them. The result table extracted badly, so only the prose figures are used. Unclear if gains are points or percent.
agent_relevance: Short verbal cues per candidate help choice; test on equal tokens before adding to the agent.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Complete chess games enable LLM become a chess master (ChessLLM)
finding: A 3B language model fine-tuned on full games reaches a middling Elo; data type matters.
numbers: Elo 1788 vs Stockfish when allowed 10 samples; won 61% vs Stockfish skill level 0, 56% at level 1, 30% at level 2. Long-game supervision beat short-round data by 350 Elo. Over 20B tokens.
limits: Ten samples and a legality filter help; Stockfish skill levels are not human Elo.
agent_relevance: Pattern volume and full-game context matter; sample a shortlist then choose (best-of-10 style).

source: Liu et al. (2026) ChessArena: a chess testbed for evaluating strategic reasoning of LLMs
finding: Asks directly whether LLMs reason strategically or only recognise patterns. No LLM beat a human-amateur engine.
numbers: 13 LLMs, over 800 games, about 30 games per model. No model beat Maia-1100; a few lost to random play (mostly illegal moves). Thinking models (o3, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Doubao-Seed-1-6-Thinking) led. Fine-tuned Qwen3-8B improved a lot and approached larger reasoners.
limits: Glicko-style ratings; prompt format affects legality; four play modes (Bullet, Blitz, Standard, Blindfold).
agent_relevance: Models without a strong pattern store fail the first step; thinking helps but stays below amateur-human level.

source: Kolasani et al. (2025) LLM CHESS: benchmarking reasoning and instruction-following in LLMs through chess
finding: Reasoning models far outperform non-reasoning models in agentic chess against a random opponent.
numbers: 50+ models. Reasoning models: average win rate 45.4%, top near 100%. Non-reasoning: 0.7%, best 3.3%. Instruction-following errors 71.9% (non-reasoning) vs 24.4% (reasoning). o4-mini (medium) picks the best move 19.5% of plies vs 4.1% for GPT-4.1-mini; blunders 4.2% vs 31.3%.
limits: Opponent is random; Elo only for a top subset.
agent_relevance: Much of LLM weakness is rule-following and state-tracking, not only move choice.

source: Kolasani et al. (2025) LLM CHESS: benchmarking reasoning and instruction-following in LLMs through chess
finding: Even the best reasoning models are only club level when rated against an engine; more reasoning effort helps, and input format matters.
numbers: Best adjusted Elo about 758 (against Dragon skills 1-5, Elo 250-750, plus skill 10 for some). Reasoning effort low to medium gives up to +15%, low to high +20%. For o4-mini (low) changing the board format raised performance by over 15%, reaching 95% for FEN. A further ablation lowered Grok 3 Mini (low) by almost 30% and raised o4-mini (low) by 10%.
limits: Elo scale is engine-specific. The last ablation is described in a short passage; its exact feature was not recorded.
agent_relevance: Cue visibility (board format) and effort give big swings; test the S0 gate against those before adding other parts.

source: Hwang et al. (2025) Can large language models develop strategic reasoning? Post-training insights from learning chess
finding: RL with a chess action-value network as dense reward beats sparse reward, yet every model plateaus far below expert level. The cause looks like missing stored chess knowledge, not missing reasoning.
numbers: Puzzle accuracy plateaus at 25-30%; expert level 60-80% (1800-Elo models reach 66.5% per Ruoss et al.). SFT on reasoning traces from o3 gave similar plateaus. Table of starting values lists instruct models at 52.0% (Qwen2.5-7B-It) and 52.4% (Llama3.1-8B-It) on one metric.
limits: Small models (3B to 8B); one RL recipe; the starting-value metric is not identified in the extracted text.
agent_relevance: Test of search without patterns: more reasoning on poor pattern knowledge stalls. Supports a memory gate before long deliberation.

source: Tang et al. (2026) Grounded chess reasoning in language models via master distillation (C1)
finding: Distilling engine reasoning into short chain-of-thought gives a 4B model that beats its teacher.
numbers: C1 reaches 48.1% from a near-zero start; teacher Gemini-3-Flash 40.8%; two orders of magnitude fewer tokens than baselines. By data size: 19.3% at 8k, 29.7% at 16k, 40.9% at 39k samples. Full fine-tuning 40.9% vs LoRA 32.1% (rank 16) and 38.8% (rank 64).
limits: Tactics themes only; one recipe; teacher is a frontier model.
agent_relevance: Compact cue-to-move chains beat long free-form reasoning on tokens.

source: Bhaskar, Cheng and Chen (2026) Language models that play chess and explain their moves (QUEEN)
finding: A 4B chess-language model that reads a strong engine's encoder and explains top candidate moves gains over 900 Elo in seven rounds.
numbers: Elo 1782 to 2697 (1782, 2024, 2187, 2346, 2539, 2434, 2559, 2697). Beats the strongest frontier model by over 600 rating points in Lichess games. Selects a different top move from Leela on 538 of 1,000 test positions.
limits: Preprint; Lichess Elos after 32 games; the engine encoder is the pattern store.
agent_relevance: Loop: shortlist candidates from a pattern encoder, look one step past each, write it down, distil. A trained recognition-guided search.

source: Dionisopoulos, Majamaki and Ammanabrolu (2026) How reasoning evolves from post-training data: an empirical study using chess
finding: Training the model to output the best move directly gives the strongest results after RL, but RL then yields reasoning that does not match the move. Multi-move trajectories give comparable results with faithful reasoning.
numbers: 7B model beats leading open-source reasoning models in chess. Share of validation tokens that are hallucinated: factual board answering 0.04%, guided synthetic 2.90%, rejection sampling 12.69%, verbalized alpha-beta 4.31%. Dataset accuracy: board answering 62.54%, verbalized alpha-beta 71.04%, best move 28.61%, best line 24.00%.
limits: Table columns read from messy text, labels may shift; custom datasets.
agent_relevance: A pure recognition target works best but its stated reasoning cannot be trusted. Audit the move and the story separately.

source: Parfenova (2026) Do chess explanations reflect model decisions? Behavioral and token-level tests of LLM reasoning faithfulness
finding: Written chess rationales often do not carry the move. With explicit move hints masked they add little over the board alone.
numbers: 200 Lichess endgame puzzles. Random but plausible explanations from other puzzles lower the probability of the correct move. Decoder recovery of the model's move drops sharply after masking. Motif-rich explanations raise recoverability without reliably raising correctness.
limits: Endgame puzzles only; accuracy tables not cleanly extracted.
agent_relevance: Irrelevant cues are costly: they shift the move. Check retrieved templates against the position.

source: Kshirsagar (2026) The weight of silence: a causal case for weights over the scratchpad in latent chess reasoning
finding: Latent thought vectors in a chess model mainly shape the weights in training; at inference they act little like a consulted scratchpad.
numbers: RL raised legality from 48% to 61%. Swapping thoughts for matched noise left performance unchanged; exact-zero vectors collapsed legality to 1% before RL vs 9% after RL.
limits: One model, independent researcher; legality, not move quality.
agent_relevance: Knowledge sits in the store (weights or memory). A prompt-only agent needs the cue in context to benefit.

source: Shen et al. (2026) Understanding reasoning from pretraining to post-training
finding: In a controlled chess pipeline, pretraining loss predicts post-RL performance. RL on hard puzzles surfaces moves that were nearly absent before.
numbers: Models from 5M to 1B parameters; slope of RL reward improves about linearly with pretraining tokens. On easy puzzles RL amplifies moves the SFT model already preferred.
limits: Chess plus one math check; small models.
agent_relevance: The pattern prior sets the ceiling for later search or RL gains.

source: Meng et al. (2024) Searchformer: beyond A* via search dynamics bootstrapping
finding: A transformer trained on search traces, then fine-tuned to shorten them, solves planning tasks with fewer search steps than its A* teacher.
numbers: Solves 93.7% of unseen Sokoban puzzles with on average 26.8% fewer search steps than A*; ten times fewer training sequences than a larger solution-only model; A* traces were 34.3% longer than Searchformer after 3 rounds.
limits: Not chess; mazes and Sokoban; classical teacher.
agent_relevance: A model can shorten search by learning where not to look: a machine analogue of templates shortening search.

source: Wen, Tang and Anderson (2025) ChessQA: evaluating large language models for chess understanding
finding: Five-level benchmark from rules to semantic description; persistent weaknesses found in all five.
numbers: Categories: Structural, Motifs, Short Tactics, Position Judgment, Semantic. No per-model numbers were read.
limits: Abstract and intro only.
agent_relevance: The ladder from rules to motifs to tactics matches a pattern-store view; use it to see which level fails first.
